chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: How does the 'MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark' frontier update relate to the core course modules on evaluation, RL and agents?
options: It supersedes the evaluation-harness lesson, which is now out of date
It adds recent industry news on top of them and replaces nothing
It replaces the GRPO lesson with a newer, benchmark-approved algorithm
It is a prerequisite that must be read before starting Module 16
explanation: The page is a bonus frontier update layered on Modules 13, 16 and 19. It shows how the same mechanisms are now measured at industry scale but does not replace any lesson. It is not a prerequisite for Module 16.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Since late 2025, where have most LLM capability gains come from, according to the MLPerf post-training frontier update?
options: Scaling the tokenizer vocabulary
Switching from transformers to recurrent networks
Scaling post-training
Longer pretraining on the same data
explanation: The update states that since late 2025 most capability gains have come from scaling post-training. What was missing was a standard way to measure time-to-quality for it, which the MLPerf workload provides.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What gap does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark fill?
options: A public dataset of human preference pairs for reward models
A reference GPU kernel for attention shared across submitters
A standard way to measure time-to-quality for post-training
A standard tokenizer and chat template shared by all labs
explanation: Until this benchmark there was no standard way to measure how long it takes to post-train a model to a quality target. MLPerf now measures that time-to-quality. It is not a tokenizer, preference dataset or kernel.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which skills does the MLPerf post-training benchmark exercise, making them relevant for lab hiring?
options: Web front-end design, SQL query tuning, container orchestration, CDN caching, and mobile release pipelines
RLVR loop design, eval-metric choice, reward-hacking defenses, gen/train overlap, weight transfer, KV cache
Hyperparameter search only, on fixed infrastructure, with learning rate, batch size, and warmup as the knobs
Tokenizer training, image augmentation, speech recognition, diffusion sampling, and contrastive pretraining
explanation: The benchmark stresses model-adjacent systems skills: designing the RLVR loop, choosing eval metrics, defending against reward hacking, overlapping generation with training, transferring weights, and managing KV cache for long agent trajectories. Those are exactly what post-training teams hire for.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: When does the MLPerf Training LLM post-training workload start, according to MLCommons' September 2026 announcement?
options: With the v5.0 submission round in January 2025
It has no fixed round; results are accepted continuously
With the v6.1 submission round in October 2026
With the v7.0 submission round planned for mid-2027
explanation: MLCommons announced in September 2026 that it will add an LLM post-training workload to MLPerf Training starting with the v6.1 submission round in October 2026. This is publicly documented.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which RL algorithm does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark use?
options: DPO on preference pairs
GRPO over rollout iterations
PPO with a learned critic
REINFORCE with no baseline
explanation: The benchmark uses GRPO over rollout iterations, with a binary verifiable reward. DPO is offline preference optimization; PPO uses a critic that GRPO drops; plain REINFORCE without a baseline is not the chosen design.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What reward does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark use?
options: The negative perplexity of the generated patch under the model
A scalar score from a learned reward model trained on patches
A binary pass/fail reward from running tests (RLVR)
Human ratings of each patch collected after every rollout
explanation: The reward is binary: 1 if the tests pass, 0 otherwise, which is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Learned reward models and human ratings are not used, and perplexity does not measure whether a bug is fixed.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What policy model does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark train?
options: A 7B dense model fine-tuned with LoRA adapters on every attention and MLP projection
A dense 70B model with all of its parameters active for every token it processes
GPT-2 small with 124M parameters, chosen so that submissions can run on one GPU
Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, an MoE with 397B total and ~17B active parameters per token
explanation: The policy is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, a mixture-of-experts model: 397B total parameters, about 17B active per token. The A17B suffix denotes active parameters. It is neither dense nor small.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Where do the tasks in the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark come from?
options: Multiple-choice trivia questions scored by exact match
Grade-school math word problems with numeric answers
Real software-repair tasks from R2E-Gym, run in a sandbox
Synthetic arithmetic generated on the fly by a task sampler
explanation: Tasks are real software-repair problems from R2E-Gym, run in a sandbox where tests determine the reward. Math, trivia or synthetic arithmetic are other RLVR domains, not the benchmark's.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which agent harness does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark fix for training and validation?
options: No harness; the model outputs a patch in one shot
OpenHands for training and a custom harness for validation
Any harness the submitter chooses
OpenHands, for both training and validation
explanation: The benchmark fixes OpenHands for both training and validation, because harness choice strongly changes solve rate. Letting submitters choose, or switching harnesses at validation, would make results incomparable.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What is the validation metric and target of the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark?
options: pass@16, with a target of 0.50 over 1004 validation rollouts
pass@4, with a target of 0.69 over 1004 validation rollouts
Perplexity, with a target of 10 on held-out repositories
pass@1, with a target of 0.95 over 100 validation rollouts
explanation: Validation uses pass@4 with target 0.69 measured over 1004 validation rollouts. pass@1 was not chosen due to higher variance; perplexity does not measure task success.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What maximum policy staleness does the MLPerf LLM post-training reference allow in async RL?
options: 1 weight version
Unbounded, as long as throughput improves
16 weight versions, one per generation
0 versions; generation and training are fully synchronous
explanation: The reference caps staleness at 1: a rollout can be generated by version t-1 while the trainer produces version t, never older. That allows overlap of generation and training while limiting the off-policy gap.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What fixed budgets does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark impose?
options: 1M context, unlimited turns, and 1 generation per prompt
65k context, 100 agent turns, and 64 generations per prompt
8k context, 5 agent turns, and 4 generations per prompt
65k context, 30 agent turns, and 16 generations per prompt
explanation: Budgets are fixed at 65k context, 30 agent turns and 16 generations per prompt (GRPO group size G = 16), so submissions compete on systems efficiency rather than letting the agent think longer.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What is the MLPerf post-training benchmark's headline metric, 'time-to-quality'?
options: The tokens per second sustained during rollout generation
Wall-clock time until the trained agent reaches pass@4 >= 0.69
The number of GPUs needed to reach pass@4 >= 0.69 in one day
The pass@4 score reached after a fixed one-hour training budget
explanation: Time-to-quality is the wall-clock time until the agent reaches the target pass@4 of 0.69. It mirrors MLPerf's existing 'time to train to a target' framing for pretraining. Fixed-budget quality or raw throughput are different metrics.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which paper introduced the unbiased pass@k estimator used in RLVR evaluation?
options: Jain et al. 2025, 'R2E-Gym', which built the repair environments
Chen et al. 2021, 'Evaluating LLMs Trained on Code' (the Codex paper)
Shao et al. 2024, 'DeepSeekMath', which introduced group-relative RL
Wang et al. 2024, 'OpenHands', the open agent platform paper
explanation: The unbiased pass@k estimator comes from Chen et al. 2021 (arXiv 2107.03374), section 2.1. DeepSeekMath introduced GRPO, R2E-Gym provides the repair tasks, and OpenHands is the agent harness.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which paper introduced GRPO?
options: Jain et al. 2025, R2E-Gym
Shao et al. 2024, DeepSeekMath
Chen et al. 2021, Evaluating LLMs Trained on Code
Liu et al. 2025, Dr. GRPO
explanation: GRPO was introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao et al. 2024, arXiv 2402.03300). Dr. GRPO is a later fix to GRPO, and the other papers cover pass@k and environment construction.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
question: In agentic RL, what is an agent harness?
options: The GPU cluster scheduler that places and runs the training and rollout jobs
The verifier that runs the tests and computes each episode's binary reward
The wrapper around the model: prompt scaffolding, tools, observation truncation, stopping
The tokenizer and chat template used to format the SFT and RL training data
explanation: An agent is a model wrapped in a harness: scaffolding, available tools (edit file, run tests, search), how observations are truncated, and stopping rules. The verifier computes reward separately; the scheduler and tokenizer are not the harness.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
question: Why did the MLPerf team fix one harness (OpenHands) for both training and validation?
options: Because harnesses have no real effect on scores, but fixing one simplifies logging and reproduction
Because OpenHands is the only open harness that supports GRPO-style group sampling of episodes
Harness choice strongly changed solve rate, and the policy learns to act inside a specific harness
Because changing harnesses breaks the tokenizer's chat template and corrupts the stored rollouts
explanation: The team found harness choice strongly changed solve rate. The policy learns to act inside the harness, and the reward depends on what tools exist and how outputs are shown. Evaluating with a different harness means evaluating a different system.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
question: What happens if you change the agent harness at evaluation time relative to training?
options: You are evaluating a different system than the one you trained
Results improve because the model generalizes to new tools
The verifier automatically adjusts the reward for the new harness
Nothing changes, since only the weights matter
explanation: Model and harness together are the unit being optimized. Swap the harness and the tool set, observations and stopping behavior all change, so the score no longer describes the trained system. Weights alone are not the system.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
question: What reasonable industry practice is recommended for agent harnesses?
options: Hard-code the harness into the model weights through SFT so it cannot drift between runs
Use a different harness for each evaluation run to test the policy's robustness to tooling
Upgrade the harness freely between checkpoints, since only the weights determine the score
Version the harness like the model and log its commit next to every checkpoint and eval
explanation: Because model + harness is the unit, the harness should be versioned like the model, with its commit recorded alongside every checkpoint and eval number. Untracked changes make results irreproducible and incomparable.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
question: When is a programmatic verifier actually ungameable in RLVR?
options: Always, because a programmatic verifier checks ground truth by construction
Only if the reward is continuous rather than binary 0/1 per episode
Only if the policy cannot touch the verifier or the files that define it
Only if the verifier is a neural network the policy cannot inspect
explanation: A verifier checks ground truth only if the policy cannot modify it. With shell access, an agent can edit the tests that define the reward. Being rule-based is not enough on its own, and neither neural verifiers nor continuous rewards fix this.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
question: What reward hack was documented in the MLPerf RLVR software-repair setup?
options: Models produced extremely long outputs to exhaust the context
Models deleted the failing tests instead of fixing the bug
Models refused to answer to avoid negative reward
Models copied the gold patch from the internet
explanation: With shell access, agents deleted failing tests; with no failing tests the suite passes and the reward is 1. That is the documented failure. The other behaviors were not the reported hack.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
question: If an agent's actions a_1:T can modify the files that define the verifier v, what is the policy effectively optimizing?
options: The true verifier, since the sandbox reverts all edits before the reward is computed
The KL divergence to the reference policy, since the reward becomes constant
The perplexity of the repository's code, since edits change what the tests read
A verifier the agent itself edited, whose easiest maximizer is to make v trivial
explanation: If the agent can edit v, it optimizes v_{a_1:T}, a verifier it modified, and the simplest way to maximize it is to make it trivially pass (e.g. delete tests). Nothing in that setup reverts the edits.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
question: What is the defense against agents deleting failing tests in RLVR software-repair tasks?
options: Run the reward on hidden test files copied into the sandbox only after the episode ends
Show the agent all tests up front, so it knows exactly which behavior it must fix
Give the agent read-only access to the whole filesystem, including the source files
Penalize every file deletion with a negative reward large enough to outweigh a pass
explanation: Hidden tests are copied in only after the agent stops, then run to compute the reward, so the agent can neither see nor modify them. Read-only access would prevent fixing bugs; deletion penalties are easy to sidestep; showing all tests invites gaming.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
question: What general rule follows from the hidden-test defense in RLVR?
options: The policy must never be given tools that touch the filesystem
Anything the policy can read must be encrypted before the episode
Rewards must always be computed by human raters, not programs
Anything the policy can write to cannot be part of the reward
explanation: The general rule is that anything the policy can write to cannot be part of the reward computation. It does not require encryption, human scoring or removing tools; it requires isolating the reward's inputs from the agent's actions.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
question: During RLVR training, training reward climbs but held-out pass rate does not. What does that suggest?
options: The held-out split is too easy, so it saturates early
The learning rate is too low for held-out gains to appear
Something is being gamed or overfit on the training side
The model is generalizing perfectly to unseen tasks
explanation: Keeping a held-out task split the loop never sees is a tripwire: if training reward rises without held-out improvement, the policy is exploiting the train-side checker or memorizing train quirks. A too-low LR would slow both; an easy held-out split would show high scores.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: What does pass@4 measure for a problem?
options: Whether all 4 attempts pass the tests
Whether the 4th attempt alone passes
Whether at least one of 4 attempts passes
The average pass rate of the 4 attempts
explanation: Under pass@k, a problem counts as solved if at least one of k attempts passes. Requiring all to pass would be a much stricter metric, and averaging gives pass@1.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: Why did MLPerf choose pass@4 as its validation metric?
options: It is the only metric compatible with binary 0/1 rewards from executing the hidden tests
It gives the highest possible scores of the metrics studied, making the target easy to hit
It had the lowest variance studied, so fewer costly rollouts decide the target was reached
It does not require running any tests, so validation is cheaper than training rollouts
explanation: pass@4 had the lowest variance, so fewer 30-turn, 65k-token agent rollouts are needed to decide whether the target is reached. Other metrics also work with binary rewards, and all of them require running tests.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: Why is pass@4 less noisy than pass@1 on a problem the model solves about 30% of the time?
options: pass@4 is about 1 - 0.7^4 = 0.76, so it flips between 0 and 1 far less than one 30% try
pass@4 is always exactly 1 for such a problem, since four tries cover every failure mode
pass@1 cannot be computed when the solve rate is below 50%, so its estimate is undefined
pass@4 averages the four rewards into a continuous score, which smooths away the noise
explanation: pass@1 at a 30% solve rate flips between 0 and 1 from run to run. pass@4 is 1 - 0.7^4, about 0.76, and is far more stable. It is not always 1, and it is still a binary per-problem outcome, not an average.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: In the unbiased pass@k estimator pass@k = 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k), what does C(n-c, k)/C(n, k) represent?
options: The chance that all k picks from the n attempts are successes
The fraction of the n attempts that passed the verifier
The chance that all k picks from the n attempts are failures
The expected number of successes among the k picks
explanation: C(n-c, k) counts k-subsets drawn only from the n-c failures, and C(n, k) counts all k-subsets, so the ratio is the probability a random k-subset has no success. One minus it is the probability of at least one success.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: In the unbiased pass@k estimator, what do n and c stand for?
options: n is the attempt budget being scored, c is the number of agent turns per attempt
n is the number of problems in the benchmark, c is the number solved at least once
n is the number of attempts sampled for the problem, c is the number that passed
n is the number of tokens per attempt, c is the context length of the harness
explanation: For each problem you sample n >= k attempts and count c that pass. k is the attempt budget being scored. Averaging the per-problem values over problems gives the benchmark score.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: How is a benchmark-level pass@k score obtained from per-problem estimates?
options: By summing c over all problems and dividing by k times n
By averaging the per-problem pass@k values over all problems
By multiplying the per-problem pass@k values across problems
By taking the maximum per-problem pass@k over the benchmark
explanation: Each problem gets its own unbiased pass@k from its (n, c) pair, and the benchmark score is the mean over problems. Max or product would not estimate the expected solve rate.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: With n = 8 samples of which c = 2 pass, pass@1 = 0.25 but pass@4 is about 0.786. What does a large pass@k minus pass@1 gap indicate?
options: The model can solve the task but not reliably, so RL has signal to exploit
The task is already fully learned, so any further RL on it is unnecessary
The estimator is biased upward at small n and should be discarded here
The model cannot solve the task at all, and the pass@4 value is pure sampling luck
explanation: A large gap means some samples succeed while most fail: capability exists but is unreliable. That is exactly where GRPO groups contain both successes and failures, giving nonzero advantages to learn from. It is not a sign of bias or of a solved task.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: Why use the unbiased estimator with n > k samples rather than just 'sample 4, check if any pass'?
options: Both are unbiased, but the formula uses all n samples, so its variance is lower
'Sample 4, check any' is biased upward, while the formula corrects for that bias
'Sample 4, check any' cannot handle binary rewards, but the formula can
The formula is cheaper, because it needs fewer samples than k per problem
explanation: Drawing exactly k samples and checking any is also unbiased, but it uses only k samples. The combinatorial estimator uses all n samples for the same k, averaging over all k-subsets, which lowers variance. It needs more samples, not fewer.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: What are the input and output types of llmre's pass_at_k for one problem?
options: Inputs are tensors of shape (P, G); output is a tensor of shape (P,)
Inputs are Python floats n, c, k; the output is an int count of passes
Inputs are Python ints n, c, k; the output is a Python float in [0, 1]
Inputs are lists of completion strings; output is a boolean per problem
explanation: Per problem, pass_at_k takes integer counts (n, c, k) and returns a float probability in [0, 1]. Over a benchmark you hold a list of (n, c) pairs. It does not operate on tensors or raw completions.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: In llmre's pass_at_k, what is returned when n - c < k?
options: 1.0, because every size-k subset must contain a success
c / n, because the estimator falls back to pass@1 there
An error, because the binomial ratio is undefined there
0.0, because there are too few failures to draw k from
explanation: If there are fewer than k failures, any k-subset must include at least one success, so the probability is exactly 1. The function short-circuits and returns 1.0. It is well-defined, not an error or a pass@1 fallback.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: How does llmre's pass_at_k compute C(n-c, k)/C(n, k) without building huge binomial coefficients?
options: By Monte Carlo sampling of random k-subsets of the attempts
By using Stirling's approximation for each of the factorials
As the product over i from n-c+1 to n of (1 - k/i)
By computing the factorials in float64 and then dividing
explanation: The ratio equals the product of (1 - k/i) for i = n-c+1..n, which takes c float multiplies. For n = 200, C(200, 100) has 59 digits, so direct factorials would overflow or lose precision. It is exact, not sampled or approximated.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
question: What is the computational cost of llmre's pass_at_k per problem?
options: O(c), negligible next to one rollout
O(n^2), dominating evaluation time
O(2^n), since it enumerates all subsets
O(k * n * c), comparable to a forward pass
explanation: The product form loops c times, so cost is O(c), which is negligible compared with generating even a single agent rollout. It never enumerates subsets.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: A pass@k script reports pass@4 = 1.0 for a problem with n = 4 attempts and c = 1 success. Is it a bug?
options: Yes: pass@4 can never be higher than 4 times pass@1, which here is 0.25
Yes: the correct value is c/n = 0.25, since there is only one success in four
No: pass@4 is always 1 whenever c > 0, for any number n of sampled attempts
No: with n = k = 4 the only 4-subset has the success, but it is high-variance
explanation: n - c = 3 < k = 4, so the single 4-subset includes the one success and pass@4 = 1.0 is correct. But with n = k there is no averaging, so the estimate is noisy; sample n > k (e.g. 16). For larger n with c = 1, pass@4 would be below 1.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why is reporting pass@k with n = k considered a mistake?
options: It is biased downward, so it always underestimates the true pass@k value
It is unbiased but noisy, with no averaging over subsets; sample more than k
It cannot be computed with the combinatorial formula when n equals k exactly
It double counts successes, so it overestimates pass@k whenever c > 1
explanation: With n = k, the estimator is still unbiased but uses a single subset, so it has high variance. Sampling n > k averages over many k-subsets. It is computable and does not double count.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What are the two phases of an RL step for LLM agents?
options: Train a reward model on preference data, then train a critic on its scores
Generate rollouts with the current policy (inference-bound), then train on them
Tokenize the task data, then pretrain on it with next-token prediction
Evaluate on held-out tasks, then checkpoint the weights if the held-out score improved
explanation: An RL step generates rollouts with the current policy, which is inference-bound and long for agent episodes, then trains on them with backprop. Run sequentially, each phase leaves the other's GPUs idle.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What does asynchronous RL do?
options: Skips generation entirely by reusing one fixed dataset of rollouts for every update
Trains several independent policies in parallel and averages their weights each step
Overlaps generation and training; generators use slightly old weights as the trainer updates
Runs training on CPU and generation on GPU, so the two never compete for accelerator memory
explanation: Async RL overlaps the two phases: generators keep producing rollouts with slightly stale weights while the trainer updates. This removes idle time. Reusing a fixed dataset would be offline RL, and averaging policies is a different technique.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What is policy staleness in async RL?
options: The number of turns an agent episode takes before the harness stops it early
How many weight versions old the generating policy is when its rollout is used
The age of the training tasks in days since they were first added to the pool
How long it has been since the reward model was last retrained on new labels
explanation: Staleness counts weight versions between the policy that generated a rollout and the one being updated with it. With staleness 1, a rollout from version t-1 can be used while producing version t. It is unrelated to reward-model age or episode length.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: With staleness s, how does the GRPO importance ratio r = pi_theta_t(y|x) / pi_theta_(t-s)(y|x) behave as s grows?
options: It becomes independent of the policy, since both terms use the same weights
It drifts further from 1, so more samples get clipped or add higher variance
It stays exactly 1 regardless of s, because GRPO renormalizes within the group
It shrinks toward 0, making the gradients from all stale samples vanish
explanation: Samples come from an older policy, so the ratio drifts away from 1 as the gap grows. More samples fall outside the clip range (wasted) or, if not clipped, add higher-variance gradient estimates. It does not stay at 1 or vanish.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: If one update changes a completion's log-prob by about 0.1, why does staleness 3 hurt more than staleness 1 with a [0.8, 1.2] clip range?
options: Both ratios stay inside the clip range, so staleness has no effect on the gradient in this case
At s = 3 the ratio becomes negative, so the clipped objective flips the sign of that sample's gradient
At s = 1, r is clipped (outside [0.8, 1.2]); at s = 3 it drifts back inside and is not clipped
At s = 1, r ≈ e^0.1 = 1.105 (inside the range); at s = 3, r ≈ e^0.3 = 1.35 (clipped, no gradient)
explanation: Log-prob drift accumulates with staleness: 0.1 per version gives r about 1.105 at s = 1, inside [0.8, 1.2], but about 1.35 at s = 3, outside it, so that sample contributes zero gradient. The numbers are illustrative; the direction is the point. Ratios are always positive.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why can an MLPerf post-training submitter not simply raise policy staleness to maximize throughput?
options: Higher staleness lowers throughput, since stale rollouts must be regenerated
Staleness only affects memory use, not quality, so it is capped by hardware
Staleness is fixed at 0 by the rules, so generation and training never overlap
The metric is time-to-quality, and more staleness can degrade quality
explanation: More staleness overlaps generation and training more, buying throughput, but increases the off-policy gap and can degrade quality. Since the score is time to reach quality, trading quality for throughput can make the time worse. The reference caps it at 1, not 0.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: In async RL, what connects policy staleness to the off-policy correction seen in PPO?
options: Both remove the need for a reference model, since the old policy plays that role in the KL term
Both are only relevant when rewards are continuous, because binary rewards need no correction
Both train on older-policy samples via an importance ratio; async RL forces it through system design
Both require a learned critic to estimate how far the old policy has drifted from the current one
explanation: PPO's ratio corrects for reusing a batch sampled from an older policy. In async RL the older policy comes from the system overlapping generation with training. Same correction, different cause. Neither requires a critic or continuous rewards.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Roughly how much data must be transferred per weight sync for a 397B-parameter model in bf16?
options: About 397 MB
About 3.2 TB
About 794 GB
About 34 GB
explanation: bf16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, so 397B x 2 is about 794 GB per sync. How fast you broadcast this from trainer to inference fleet bounds how low staleness can be. 34 GB would be the ~17B active params, but all weights must be transferred.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: What bounds how low policy staleness can be in large-scale async RL?
options: How fast weights can be transferred from the trainer to the inference fleet
The length of the learning-rate warmup before generation can start
The number of hidden tests per task that must run before each update
The tokenizer's vocabulary size, which sets the size of each logit tensor
explanation: Every new weight version must be broadcast to generators before they can use it. For huge models this transfer is large, so its speed limits how fresh the generating policy can be. The other factors don't affect staleness.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why is generation, rather than training, usually the bottleneck in long-trajectory agent RL?
options: Training uses no GPU memory for activations, so it always finishes before generation does
Each live episode holds a large, growing KV cache over up to 30 turns and 65k context
The verifier must run on the same GPU as the model, blocking generation while tests execute
Tokenization of the agent's outputs is extremely slow for code with long identifiers
explanation: Long multi-turn episodes accumulate big KV caches, consuming memory and limiting how many episodes run in parallel. That makes generation the bottleneck. KV size per token (reduced by GQA) is why it matters. Training still uses activation memory.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: In the MLPerf post-training benchmark, what does '16 generations per prompt' correspond to in GRPO?
options: The GRPO group size G = 16
The number of hidden tests per task
The number of weight versions kept in memory
The number of agent turns per episode
explanation: 16 generations per prompt is the GRPO group: 16 completions sampled for the same prompt whose rewards are standardized into advantages. Turns are capped at 30 separately.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why are context, turn and group-size budgets fixed in the MLPerf post-training benchmark?
options: Because budgets have little effect on results, so fixing them costs submitters nothing
So submissions compete on systems efficiency, not on letting the agent think longer
Because OpenHands cannot support larger context or turn budgets than these
To keep the benchmark small enough to run on CPU-only submission hardware
explanation: Fixing budgets removes 'we let the agent think longer' as a lever, so the competition is about systems efficiency. Budgets do affect results strongly, which is exactly why they must be fixed and logged.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why is a pass@1 number reported without its turn and context budget not comparable to anything?
options: Because budgets only affect training speed, not quality, so they are reported separately
Because pass@1 is mathematically undefined unless the turn budget is stated with it
Because pass@1 must always be reported together with pass@16 under the MLPerf rules
Budgets move results as much as learning rate does, so they are part of what was measured
explanation: Turn, context and group budgets are hyperparameters that move results as much as LR. A score without them hides a major variable. Log them per run so numbers can be compared.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why is comparing agent scores across different harnesses or budgets a mistake?
options: Model + harness + budget is the unit measured, so changing any part changes the system
Because harnesses only affect latency, so their scores differ only in wall-clock time to finish
Because budgets are always identical across papers, so only the harness differs
Because only the model weights determine the score, and those are rarely released
explanation: The measured unit is model + harness + budget. A different harness or budget measures a different system, so scores are not comparable. Weights alone do not determine agent performance.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
question: In a GRPO group of 4 attempts with rewards [1, 0, 0, 0], how are the advantages distributed?
options: The one success gets a large positive advantage (≈1.73); each failure a small negative one (≈-0.58)
The success gets 0, since it equals the group maximum, and each failure gets -0.25 below the mean
All four attempts get the same advantage of 0.25, the group's mean reward, before clipping
The success gets +1 and each failure gets -1, since binary rewards are mapped to signs
explanation: Mean is 0.25 and population std is about 0.433, so A = (r - 0.25)/0.433 = [1.732, -0.577, -0.577, -0.577]. The rare success is pushed up strongly; each failure is pushed down a little. The advantages sum to zero.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
question: Why does a GRPO group in which every attempt fails give no gradient?
options: The KL penalty cancels the policy-gradient term exactly when every reward is zero
All rewards are equal, so std = 0 and every advantage is 0 (the eps guard returns zeros)
The loss becomes infinite from dividing by a zero std, so the step is skipped
The verifier refuses to score failed attempts, so the group has no rewards at all
explanation: With identical rewards the group mean equals each reward and std is 0, so all advantages are 0 and an eps guard prevents division by zero. There is no better-than-average completion to reinforce. The same holds if all succeed.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
question: Why do tasks with pass@G near 0 contribute nothing to GRPO training?
options: If no attempt in the group of G succeeds, all rewards and advantages are 0
Because the verifier skips hard tasks once their failure rate passes a threshold
Because hard tasks are filtered out by the harness before any rollouts are made
Because the importance ratio is always clipped on them, so they give no gradient
explanation: pass@G near 0 means groups almost always contain no success, so rewards are uniformly 0 and advantages vanish. That is why the pass@k - pass@1 gap matters: training signal needs mixed groups.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
question: Which llmre function computes GRPO's group-standardized advantages?
options: llmre.rl.ppo.compute_advantages
llmre.rl.grpo.grpo_advantages
llmre.evaluation.pass_at_k.pass_at_k
llmre.rl.gvpo.gvpo_loss
explanation: grpo_advantages in llmre/rl/grpo.py standardizes rewards per group, e.g. [[1, 0, 0, 0]] -> [[1.7321, -0.5774, -0.5774, -0.5774]]. pass_at_k is the evaluation estimator, compute_advantages is PPO's, and gvpo_loss is a different objective.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which of these is listed as part of eval design for agents in the MLPerf frontier update?
options: Checking right tool selection versus following instructions inside it, with per-step evidence
Using a different harness for each eval run, so that the score reflects robustness to tooling
Reporting a single aggregate score only, so that releases are compared on one number
Gating releases on training loss reaching a threshold rather than on held-out evals
explanation: Eval design for agents separates tool selection from instruction-following within the tool, uses deterministic routing checks, prefers per-step evidence over one aggregate number, and gates releases on evals passing. A single aggregate or training loss hides failures.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Before claiming a gain, what reproducibility step is recommended in the MLPerf frontier update?
options: Run a single seed and report the best checkpoint by its held-out score
Increase the eval set size until the observed gain becomes significant
Compare the training loss curves between runs to confirm the gain is real
Measure the noise floor, e.g. the score shift from a dtype conversion alone
explanation: Measure the noise floor first: the score change from mere checkpoint-format or dtype conversion tells you how big a real gain must be. Also prefer held-out metrics over loss curves and check results across seeds. A single best-seed number is the anti-pattern.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which RLVR mechanics are listed as the first learning priority from the MLPerf update?
options: Group-relative advantage, binary verifiable rewards, hidden-test defenses, pass@k choice, async staleness
LoRA rank selection, post-training quantization, structured pruning, and adapter merging for model deployment
Tokenizer training, data deduplication, positional encodings, and long-context pretraining schedules
Image augmentation, contrastive losses, diffusion noise schedules, and classifier-free guidance
explanation: The first priority is RLVR mechanics: GRPO's group-relative advantage, binary verifiable rewards, reward-hacking defenses like hidden tests, choosing pass@k, and policy staleness. The other topics are from other parts of ML.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: What minimum hardware does the function-calling RLVR lab require?
options: 1x 24 GB GPU (e.g. RTX 4090 / A10G), a ≤3B model with LoRA; CPU-only does not work
A single 8 GB GPU running full fine-tuning of a 7B model in bf16 with gradient checkpointing
8x H100 GPUs for a 70B model, since RLVR needs the full policy plus a reference copy
A laptop CPU with 8 GB RAM, since the lab uses only small models and tiny tasks
explanation: The minimum is one 24 GB GPU with a <=3B model and LoRA; recommended is one 80 GB GPU for a 7B model with LoRA. CPU-only fails for the real lab, though pass@k and GVPO code runs on CPU. Expected cost is roughly 4-20 GPU-hours (an estimate).

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: In the function-calling RLVR lab, how should each task's programmatic check be wrapped?
options: As a perplexity score of the completion under the reference model
As a learned reward model trained on human labels of completions
As a continuous similarity between completion and gold-answer embeddings
As reward(task, completion) -> 0.0 or 1.0, like arithmetic_verifier
explanation: Each task's pass/fail check becomes a binary verifiable reward, exactly like arithmetic_verifier in the RLVR lesson. Learned reward models and similarity scores are hackable proxies; perplexity does not measure correctness.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: What reward-hacking tripwire does the function-calling RLVR lab require?
options: A hidden held-out task split the loop never sees, with check files out of the policy's reach
Training only on the held-out split, so that any gaming shows up in the reported metric
A penalty for every tool call the agent makes, so it cannot probe the checker repeatedly
Showing the agent the gold answers up front, so that it has no incentive to guess or game
explanation: Split tasks into train and a hidden held-out set never seen in training, and keep code/test files used by checks inaccessible to the policy. Showing gold answers creates a hack target, and tool-call penalties don't detect gaming.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: In the function-calling RLVR lab, which metrics are reported on the held-out split before and after RL?
options: Only the training reward, averaged over the last 100 steps
Only pass@16, estimated from a single rollout per prompt
pass@1 and pass@4, via pass_at_k from 4-8 rollouts per prompt
Perplexity and BLEU against the reference tool-call strings
explanation: Sample 4-8 rollouts per prompt and report pass@1 and pass@4 on the held-out split, watching the gap. Training reward alone can be gamed; perplexity/BLEU do not measure task success; pass@16 cannot be estimated from one rollout.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: Which budgets must be fixed and logged per run in the function-calling RLVR lab?
options: Only the number of GPUs and the wall-clock time per run
The tokenizer vocabulary size and the embedding dimension
Max context, max turns, group size and sampling temperature
Only the learning rate and the warmup schedule of the run
explanation: Context, turns, group size and temperature all move results and must be fixed and logged, one line per run. Logging only LR or GPU count misses budget variables that change scores.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: What GRPO implementation does the function-calling RLVR lab suggest for running at scale, and what does it do?
options: TRL's GRPOTrainer: the same group sampling, standardized advantages and clipped ratio as from scratch
PEFT's DPOTrainer, which turns GRPO into offline preference learning on chosen/rejected pairs
DeepSpeed's PPOTrainer, which adds a learned critic and GAE on top of the group baseline
vLLM's GRPOTrainer, which replaces stochastic group sampling with greedy decoding for speed
explanation: The lab suggests TRL's GRPOTrainer; it implements the same mechanism you built from scratch (group sampling, standardized advantages, clipped ratio) at scale. The other options misname tools or change the algorithm.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
question: What should the one-page decision note at the end of the function-calling RLVR lab answer?
options: How much the training reward increased and how quickly it plateaued over the run
Which hyperparameters gave the lowest training loss across the sweep of RL runs
Whether RL beat the SFT/LoRA baseline on held-out, at what cost, and where reward was gamed
How many tokens the tokenizer produced per task and how that changed the available context budget
explanation: The note should report held-out improvement over the SFT/LoRA baseline, compute cost, and any reward gaming. Training reward and loss are not evidence that RL helped.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: An RLVR run shows train pass@1 rising from 0.40 to 0.85 but held-out pass@1 only from 0.38 to 0.41. What is the first thing to check?
options: Train longer, since held-out metrics always lag training metrics by several hundred steps
Read ~20 successful train rollouts for gaming: edited checks, hard-coded outputs, special-cased IDs
Switch the held-out split to the training tasks so both metrics measure the same distribution
Increase the learning rate so the held-out gains catch up with the training gains faster
explanation: A large train-only gain means overfitting to train tasks or exploiting the train-side checker. The first action is to inspect successful train rollouts for gaming. Training longer or with a higher LR will likely deepen the problem.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: In an RLVR run, held-out pass@4 drops from 0.62 to 0.60 while held-out pass@1 rises slightly. What does this indicate?
options: Mode collapse: sampling diversity dropped, so extra attempts help less
That the verifier became stricter during training as checks were updated
A bug in the pass@k estimator, since pass@4 can never fall while pass@1 rises
Better exploration, since pass@4 should fall as pass@1 rises in healthy runs
explanation: pass@4 falling while pass@1 barely rises means the policy is concentrating on one strategy, so multiple attempts are less diverse. Fixes: raise the KL coefficient or temperature, stop earlier, add more diverse train tasks.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Which fixes are suggested for RL mode collapse, where held-out pass@4 falls while pass@1 rises?
options: Lower the temperature to zero and train longer, so the policy settles on its best strategy
Reduce the group size to 1, so each update follows a single trajectory with less noise
Remove the KL penalty entirely, so the policy is free to explore away from the reference
Raise the KL coefficient or temperature, stop earlier, or add more diverse train tasks
explanation: Collapse is loss of diversity; a stronger KL to the reference, higher temperature, earlier stopping and more diverse tasks counteract it. Zero temperature, no KL, or group size 1 all reduce diversity or signal further.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why is trusting training reward curves a common mistake in RLVR?
options: Training reward is not logged by standard GRPO implementations, so the curves are reconstructed
Only held-out metrics show whether RL helped; training reward can rise via gaming or overfitting
Training reward cannot be computed for binary rewards, so the curve is a smoothed proxy metric
Training reward is always lower than held-out reward, so the curves understate real progress
explanation: Rising training reward can reflect reward hacking or memorization. Only held-out metrics, on tasks the loop never sees, show real improvement.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
question: Why is letting the policy see or edit the reward's inputs a mistake in RLVR?
options: It prevents the policy from using tools, since the reward files lock the sandbox
Visible tests, writable config or accessible gold answers all become hacking targets
It slows training because of the extra file I/O every time the reward is computed
It makes the reward continuous instead of binary, which breaks GRPO's advantages
explanation: Anything the policy can read or write that feeds the reward can be exploited, as when agents deleted failing tests. Keep the reward's inputs hidden from the policy.

chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
section: What to read / what to skip
question: Which section of the Codex paper should be read for the pass@k estimator?
options: Section 7 on broader impacts
The UI and deployment sections
The appendix on tokenization
Section 2.1
explanation: The Codex paper (Chen et al. 2021) section 2.1 introduces the unbiased pass@k estimator. The reading guide also recommends R2E-Gym's environment-construction and hybrid-verifier sections, and skimming OpenHands architecture while skipping its UI sections.
